title: Bekhorot 43
description: Rava closes the tumtum’s ḥalitza, and a new chapter opens on the blemishes of priests: why the Torah lists blemishes for priests, offerings and the firstborn alike, the priest who is “not equal among the seed of Aaron,” odd shapes of the head, the hunchback, the bald, the gibben and the ḥarum.
topics: 💍 Rava: what Rabbi Yehuda and his son Rabbi Yosei disagree on about a tumtum’s ḥalitza
📖 Chapter 7 begins: every blemish of an animal also disqualifies a priest
🔁 “Scabbed” and “scabbed”: a verbal analogy that is free, and why the Torah still lists blemishes twice
⚖️ Rava: priest, offerings and firstborn, why none can be learned from the others
👤 “A man who is equal among the seed of Aaron”: three levels of disqualification
🧑‍🦲 Shapes of the head, humps and the kere’aḥ: Rava’s two versions
🧐 The gibben: no eyebrows, overhanging eyebrows, or a crooked spine; “Are you Shimi?”
👃 The ḥarum and the eyes: Rabbi Yosei, “you have gone too far”

a2.he: וְלַחְלוֹץ שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹם אַחִים, אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.

a4.he: מַתְנִי׳ מוּמִין אֵלּוּ, בֵּין קְבוּעִין בֵּין עוֹבְרִים — פּוֹסְלִין בָּאָדָם, וְיָתֵר עֲלֵיהֶן: הַכִּילוֹן, וְהַלַּפְתָּן, וְהַמַּקָּבָן, וְשֶׁרֹאשׁוֹ שָׁקוּט, וּסְקִיפַת.

a5.he: וּבַעֲלֵי חֲטָרוֹת — רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מַכְשִׁיר, וַחֲכָמִים פּוֹסְלִין. הַקֵּרֵחַ פָּסוּל. אֵיזֶהוּ קֵרֵחַ? כֹּל שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שִׁיטָה שֶׁל שֵׂעָר מוּקֶּפֶת מֵאוֹזֶן לְאוֹזֶן, אִם יֵשׁ לוֹ — הֲרֵי זֶה כָּשֵׁר.

a6.he: גְּמָ׳ אַמַּאי? וְהָאִיכָּא יַבֶּלֶת, דְּלָא כְּתִיב בְּאוֹרָיְיתָא בְּאָדָם! וְתוּ: דַּק תְּבַלּוּל, דְּלָא כְּתִיבִי בִּבְהֵמָה!

a7.he: מֵילָף יָלְפִי מֵהֲדָדֵי, דְּתַנְיָא: בָּאָדָם לֹא נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ יַבֶּלֶת, בַּבְּהֵמָה לֹא נֶאֱמַר דַּק תְּבַלּוּל, מִנַּיִן לִיתֵּן אֶת הָאָמוּר שֶׁל זֶה בָּזֶה וְאֶת הָאָמוּר שֶׁל זֶה בָּזֶה? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״גָּרָב״ ״גָּרָב״, ״יַלֶּפֶת״ ״יַלֶּפֶת״ לִגְזֵירָה שָׁוָה.

a8.he: מַפְנֵי, דְּאִי לָא מַפְנֵי, אִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: אָדָם מִבְּהֵמָה לָא יָלֵיף, שֶׁכֵּן הִיא עַצְמָהּ קְרֵיבָה לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ; בְּהֵמָה מֵאָדָם לָא יָלְפָא, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה בְּמִצְוֹת.

a9.he: לָאיֵי, אַפְנוֹיֵי מַפְנֵי, לִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא ״יַלֶּפֶת״ וְלָא בָּעֵי ״גָּרָב״, וַאֲנָא אָמֵינָא: וּמָה יַלֶּפֶת דְּלָא מְאִיסָא הָוֵי מוּמָא, גָּרָב דִּמְאִיס לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן? ״גָּרָב״ ״גָּרָב״ דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא לְמָה לִי? לְאַפְנוֹיֵי.

a10.he: וְלִכְתְּבִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא כּוּלְּהוּ בְּחַד, וְגָרָב וְיַלֶּפֶת הָכָא וְהָכָא, וְלֵילְפוּ מֵחֲדָא!

a11.he: אַהֵיָיא בְּהֵי לִיכְתֹּב רַחֲמָנָא? אִי כְּתַב בְּאָדָם, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: כֹּל דְּפָסוּל בְּאָדָם פָּסוּל בִּבְהֵמָה, קָלוּט וְחוּטִין דְּלֵיתַנְהוּ בְּאָדָם, בִּבְהֵמָה נָמֵי לָא לִיפַּסְלוּ.

a12.he: וְלִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא כּוּלְּהוּ בִּבְהֵמָה, הָוֵה אָמֵינָא: כֹּל דְּפָסוּל בִּבְהֵמָה פָּסוּל בְּאָדָם, גִּבֵּן וְחָרוּם דְּלֵיתַנְהוּ בִּבְהֵמָה — בְּאָדָם נָמֵי לָא לִיפַּסְלוּ.

a13.he: וְלִכְתְּבִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא כּוּלְּהוּ בְּחַד, וְהָנָךְ דְּלֵיתַנְהוּ בְּאִידַּךְ — לִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא בִּבְהֵמָה, וְהָנָךְ דְּלֵיתַנְהוּ בְּאִידַּךְ — לִכְתּוֹב בְּאָדָם, וְגָרָב וְיַלֶּפֶת — הָכָא וְהָכָא, וְלֵילְפִי מֵהֲדָדֵי.

a14.he: אֶלָּא, כְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, דְּתָנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל: כׇּל פָּרָשָׁה שֶׁנֶּאֶמְרָה וְנִשְׁנֵית — לֹא נִשְׁנֵית אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל דָּבָר שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ בָּהּ.

a15.he: אָמַר רָבָא: לְמָה לִי דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא מוּם בְּאָדָם, מוּם בְּקָדָשִׁים, מוּם בִּבְכוֹר?

a16.he: צְרִיכָא, דְּאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא מוּם בְּאָדָם, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה בְּמִצְווֹת. אָדָם מִבְּכוֹר בְּהֵמָה לָא אָתֵי, שֶׁכֵּן הוּא עַצְמוֹ קָרֵב לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ.

a17.he: קָדָשִׁים מִבְּכוֹר לָא אָתֵי, שֶׁכֵּן קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ מֵרֶחֶם.

a18.he: אָדָם מִקֳּדָשִׁים לָא אָתֵי, שֶׁכֵּן הֵן עַצְמָן קְרֵיבִין. בְּכוֹר מִקֳּדָשִׁים לָא אָתֵי, שֶׁכֵּן קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ מְרוּבָּה.

a19.he: חֲדָא מֵחֲדָא לָא אָתְיָא, תֵּיתֵי חֲדָא מִתַּרְתֵּי? מֵהֵי תֵּיתֵי?! לָא לִכְתֹּב רַחֲמָנָא בִּבְכוֹר, וְתֵיתֵי מֵהָנָךְ? מָה לְהָנָךְ שֶׁכֵּן קְדוּשָּׁתָן מְרוּבָּה, וְנוֹהֲגִין בִּפְשׁוּטִין.

a20.he: בְּקָדָשִׁים, וְתֵיתֵי מֵהָנָךְ? מָה לְהָנָךְ שֶׁכֵּן קְדוּשָּׁתָן מֵאֲלֵיהֶן!

a21.he: בְּאָדָם, וְתֵיתֵי מֵהָנָךְ? מָה לְהָנָךְ שֶׁכֵּן הֵן עַצְמָן קְרֵיבִין לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ! צְרִיכִי.

a22.he: יָתֵר עֲלֵיהֶן בְּאָדָם. מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי? אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, דְּאָמַר קְרָא: ״כֹּל אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם מִזֶּרַע אַהֲרֹן״, אִישׁ שֶׁשָּׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן.

b1.he: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין מוּמָא לְשֶׁאֵינוֹ שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן? אִיכָּא מִשּׁוּם אַחוֹלֵי עֲבוֹדָה: מוּמָא מַחֵיל עֲבוֹדָה, דִּכְתִיב: ״מוּם בּוֹ וְלֹא יְחַלֵּל״, שֶׁאֵינוֹ שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן לָא מַחֵיל עֲבוֹדָה.

b2.he: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין שֶׁאֵינוֹ שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן, וּמִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן? אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ עֲשֵׂה.

b3.he: כִּילוֹן — דְּדָמֵי רֵישֵׁיהּ לְאַכְלָא, ״לַפְתָּא״ — דְּדָמֵי רֵישֵׁיהּ לְגַדְגָּלִידָא דְּלִיפְתָּא, תָּנָא: וְצַוָּארוֹ עוֹמֵד בְּאֶמְצַע רֹאשׁוֹ.

b4.he: מַקָּבָן — דְּדָמֵי רֵישֵׁיהּ לְמַקָּבָן, ״וְשֶׁרֹאשׁוֹ שָׁקוּט״ — מִלְּפָנָיו, ״וּסְקִיפָת״ — מֵאֲחוֹרָיו, כִּדְאָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי: שְׁקִיל פִּיסָּא. תָּנָא: וְצַוָּארוֹ שָׁקוּט וְשָׁמוּט. ״שָׁקוּט״ — דַּחֲבִיס מִחְבָּס, ״שָׁמוּט״ — דַּאֲרִיךְ וּשְׁמִיט.

b5.he: וּבַעֲלֵי חֲטָרוֹת רַבִּי יְהוּדָה כּוּ׳. דְּאִית בֵּיהּ עֶצֶם, כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּפָסְלָא. כִּי פְּלִיגִי — דְּלֵית בֵּיהּ עֶצֶם: מָר סָבַר — הָא אֵינוֹ שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן, וּמָר סָבַר — קִרְקוּרָא דְּבִישְׂרָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא.

b6.he: הַקֵּרֵחַ פָּסוּל. אָמַר רָבָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין לוֹ לְאַחֲרָיו וְיֵשׁ לוֹ לְפָנָיו, אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹ לְאַחֲרָיו — כָּשֵׁר, וְכׇל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְאַחֲרָיו וְאֵין לוֹ לְפָנָיו.

b7.he: וְאִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי אַסֵּיפָא, וְאִם יֵשׁ לוֹ — הֲרֵי זֶה כָּשֵׁר. אָמַר רָבָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְאַחֲרָיו וְאֵין לוֹ לְפָנָיו, אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹ בֵּין לְאַחֲרָיו בֵּין לְפָנָיו — פָּסוּל, וְכׇל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ לְפָנָיו וְאֵין לוֹ לְאַחֲרָיו, וּדְאֵין לוֹ כְּלָל — דְּפָסוּל.

b8.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הַקַּרְחָנִין וְהַנַּנָּסִין וְהַזַּבְלְגָנִין — פְּסוּלִין, לְפִי שֶׁאֵינָן שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן. קַרְחָנִין — תְּנֵינָא! נַנָּסִין — תְּנֵינָא!

b9.he: זַבְלְגָנִין אִיצְטְרִיךְ לֵיהּ לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן, וּמַהוּ דְּתֵימָא מִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן.

b10.he: וְהָא כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא מִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן (אִיתְנָא) [מִיתְנָא] קָתָנֵי, וְשֶׁנָּשְׁרוּ רִיסֵי עֵינָיו פָּסוּל מִפְּנֵי מַרְאִית הָעַיִן! מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: תָּנֵי חֲדָא, וְהוּא הַדִּין לְכוּלְּהוּ.

b11.he: וְהָא כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא מִיהְדָּר וּמִיתְנָא, קָא הָדַר וְתָנֵי: וְשֶׁנִּיטְּלוּ שִׁינָּיו פָּסוּל מִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן! אֶלָּא, לְאַפּוֹקֵי מֵהָא דְּתַנְיָא, דְּתַנְיָא: הַקַּרְחָנִין וְהַנַּנָּסִין וְהַזַּבְלְגָנִין כְּשֵׁרִים, וְלֹא אָמְרוּ פָּסוּל אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן.

b12.he: מַאן הַאי תַּנָּא? רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא, דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: ״הַכֹּהֲנִים״ — לְרַבּוֹת הַקַּרְחָנִין.

b13.he: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין לוֹ גְּבִינִין, אוֹ אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא גְּבִין אֶחָד — זֶהוּ גִּבֵּן הָאָמוּר בְּתוֹרָה. רַבִּי דּוֹסָא אוֹמֵר: (שֶׁגְּבִינִין) [שֶׁגְּבִינָיו] שׁוֹכְבִין. רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן אַנְטִיגְנוֹס אוֹמֵר: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁנֵי גַּבִּין וּשְׁתֵּי שִׁדְרָאוֹת.

b14.he: גְּמָ׳ וְגִבֵּן — דְּאֵין לוֹ מַשְׁמַע? וּרְמִינְהוּ: ״גִּבֵּן״ — שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ גְּבִינִין הַרְבֵּה, אֵין לוֹ גְּבִינִין, אוֹ אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא גְּבִין אַחַד — מִנַּיִן? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אוֹ גִבֵּן״. אָמַר רָבָא: זֶהוּ מִדְרָשׁ ״אוֹ גִּבֵּן״.

b15.he: רַבִּי דּוֹסָא אוֹמֵר כּוּ׳. לְמֵימְרָא דְּחָיֵי? וְהָא אִיתְּמַר: הַמַּפֶּלֶת בְּרִיָּה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ שְׁנֵי גַּבִּין וּשְׁתֵּי שִׁדְרָאוֹת, וְאָמַר רַב: בָּאִשָּׁה — אֵינוֹ וָולָד, בַּבְּהֵמָה — אָסוּר בַּאֲכִילָה!

b16.he: כְּבָר רְמָא נִיהֲלֵיהּ רַב שִׁימִי בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב, וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: שִׁימִי אֶת! אֶלָּא בְּשֶׁשִּׁדְרָתוֹ עֲקוּמָּה.

b17.he: מַתְנִי׳ הֶחָרוּם פָּסוּל. אֵיזֶהוּ חָרוּם? הַכּוֹחֵל שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו כְּאַחַת. שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו לְמַעְלָה, וּשְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו לְמַטָּה, עֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַעְלָה וְעֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַטָּה, רוֹאֶה אֶת הַחֶדֶר וְאֶת הָעֲלִיָּיה כְּאֶחָד, סָכֵי שֶׁמֶשׁ, וְהַזַּגְדָּן, וְהַצַּיְרָן, וְשֶׁנָּשְׁרוּ רִיסֵי עֵינָיו — פָּסוּל מִפְּנֵי מַרְאִית הָעַיִן.

b18.he: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״חָרוּם״ — שֶׁחוֹטְמוֹ שָׁקוּעַ, חוֹטְמוֹ סוֹלֵד, חוֹטְמוֹ בּוֹלֵם, חוֹטְמוֹ נוֹטֵף, מִנַּיִן? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אוֹ חָרוּם״. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אֵין ״חָרוּם״ אֶלָּא הַכּוֹחֵל שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו כְּאַחַת. אָמְרוּ לוֹ: הִפְלַגְתָּ,

messages.text: Continued from 42b. Rabbi Yehuda and his son Rabbi Yosei both rule that a tumtum does not perform ḥalitza, and the Gemara asked what difference there is between them. Rava answers.

There is a practical difference with regard to disqualifying the widow, through his ḥalitza, from entering into levirate marriage in a case where there are other brothers. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that this individual is certainly a eunuch whose condition is caused naturally, his ḥalitza is of no effect whatsoever, and therefore she may enter into levirate marriage with one of the other brothers. Conversely, according to Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, since it is possible that he is not a eunuch and his ḥalitza is valid, she is forbidden to the other brothers as their brother’s wife.

notes.he: אם יש עמו אחים הגונים והלך הוא וחלץ לה לרבי יהודה לאו כלום עבד ולא פסלה מן האחין רצה אחד מן האחין לייבם מייבם ולרבי יוסי דמחזיק ליה בספק פסלה מן האחין דשמא חליצתו חליצה ואין אחד מן האחין יכול לייבמה דכיון דלא בנה שוב לא יבנה אלא חוזרין וחולצין לה:
notes.en: To disqualify where there are brothers: if there are fit brothers with him and he went and performed ḥalitza with her, according to Rabbi Yehuda he has done nothing at all and has not disqualified her from the brothers; if one of the brothers wishes to take her in levirate marriage, he may. According to Rabbi Yosei, who treats him as an uncertainty, he has disqualified her from the brothers, since perhaps his ḥalitza is a valid ḥalitza, and none of the brothers can take her in levirate marriage, for once he did not build [his brother’s house], he may not build it again. Rather, they perform ḥalitza with her again.

messages.text: And there is also a practical difference between their opinions with regard to performing ḥalitza with the widow in a case where there are no brothers other than this tumtum. According to Rabbi Yehuda, ḥalitza is not necessary in this case, as she requires ḥalitza only if her late husband had brothers who are obligated to perform levirate marriage, and this individual is definitely a eunuch whose condition is caused naturally. By contrast, Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, maintains that he must perform ḥalitza with her, in case he is a male and not a eunuch.

notes.he: אם אין אחין אלא טומטום לרבי יהודה מיפטרא בולא כלום דהא ודאי סריס הוא וכליתיה דמי ולר' יוסי בעיא חליצה שמא לאו סריס הוא והאי דקאמר לא יחלוץ במקום אחין קאמר:
notes.en: And to perform ḥalitza where there are no brothers: if there are no brothers but the tumtum, according to Rabbi Yehuda she is released with nothing at all, since he is certainly a eunuch and is as if he did not exist. According to Rabbi Yosei she requires ḥalitza, since perhaps he is not a eunuch; and when he said “he does not perform ḥalitza,” he said it of a case where there are brothers.

notes.he: הדרן עלך על אלו מומין
notes.en: We will return to you, Al Elu Mumin [the end of chapter 6].

messages.text: הדרן עלך על אלו מומין · We will return to you, chapter Al Elu Mumin.
Chapter 7 · מומין אלו (Mumin Elu): the blemishes that disqualify a priest from the Temple service.
Mishna

Concerning these blemishes which were taught with regard to an animal, whether they are permanent or transient, they also disqualify in the case of a person, i.e., they disqualify a priest from performing the Temple service.

notes.he: האמורין בבכור פוסלין לכהן לעבודה:
notes.en: Mishna. These blemishes: those stated regarding the firstborn disqualify a priest from the service.

notes.he: כל זמן שהן בו:
notes.en: Whether permanent or transient: for as long as they are on him.

notes.he: דחשבינן בבהמה:
notes.en: These blemishes: which we count for an animal.

notes.dh: בין קבועין ובין עוברין פסולין באדם
notes.he: בכהנים:
notes.en: Whether permanent or transient, they disqualify in a person: in priests.

messages.text: And in addition to those blemishes, there are other blemishes that apply only to a priest: One whose head is pointed, narrow above and wide below; and one whose head is turnip-like, wide above and narrow below; and one whose head is hammer-like, with his forehead protruding;

notes.he: מפרש בגמרא:
notes.en: The kilon, the lifta and the makkavan: explained in the Gemara.

notes.he: דפסולי[ם] באדם ולא בבהמה הכילון כו':
notes.en: And in addition to them: which disqualify in a person and not in an animal: the kilon, etc.

messages.text: and one whose head has an indentation; and one wherein the back of his head protrudes.

notes.he: מפרש בגמרא:
notes.en: And one whose head is shakut, and the sekifat: explained in the Gemara.

messages.text: And with regard to those with humped backs, Rabbi Yehuda deems them fit for service and the Rabbis deem them disqualified.

notes.he: פלוגתא אבל הנך כילון וליפתם וכולהו דברי הכל:
notes.en: And those with humps: this is a dispute; but those others, the kilon, the lifta and all of them, are agreed by everyone.

notes.he: חלדרוב"ש:
notes.en: Ḥatarot [humps]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)

messages.text: The kere’aḥ is disqualified from performing the Temple service. What is a kere’aḥ? It is anyone who does not have a row of hair encircling his head from ear to ear.
If he has a row of hair from ear to ear, that person is fit for service.
Gemara

Why does the mishna say that all the blemishes that disqualify an animal disqualify a priest as well? But there is the blemish of a wart, which is not written in the Torah with regard to a person but is written with regard to an animal (see Leviticus 22:22).
messages.quote: they also disqualify in the case of a person

verse.he: עַוֶּרֶת אוֹ שָׁבוּר אוֹ־חָרוּץ אוֹ־יַבֶּלֶת אוֹ גָרָב אוֹ יַלֶּפֶת לֹא־תַקְרִיבוּ אֵלֶּה לַיהֹוָה וְאִשֶּׁה לֹא־תִתְּנוּ מֵהֶם עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Anything blind, or injured, or maimed, or with a wen, boil-scar, or scurvy—such you shall not offer to GOD; you shall not put any of them on the altar as offerings by fire to GOD.

notes.he: פסולין באדם:
notes.en: Gemara. Why: are they disqualifying in a person?

notes.he: דלא כתיבא באדם:
notes.en: But there is a wart: which is not written regarding a person.

notes.he: ה"נ הוי מצי למיפרך מחרוץ דלא כתיב באדם ושייך באדם חוטין ובמקום עצם כמו בבהמה וכן נתוק וכרות לא כתיבי באדם וגבן לא כתיב בבהמה ואע"ג דשייך [בבהמה] למאן דמפרש לקמן ששדרתו עקומה ולא מוקי לה בגביני עיניו וא"ת אין לו ביצים או שאין לו אלא ביצה אחת דתנן לעיל (בכורות דף מ.) גבי בהמה הרי זה [מום] ואין [זה] אלא ממרוח אשך דקאמר ת"ק לקנן בפירקין אין לו ביצים או שאין לו אלא ביצה אחת זהו מרוח אשך האמור בתורה וילפינן בהמה מאדם בג"ש דבסמוך תינח לת"ק אלא לרבי ישמעאל ור"ע דאמרי חסר אשך מיבעי ליה מנא להו דאינהו גופייהו חשבי ליה מומא בפירקין דלעיל ואי נפקא לן ממומין שבגלוי ואינן חוזרין א"כ לת"ק למה לי קרא להכי ואינהו נמי הוה מוקמי קרא להכי אי לאו משום דחסר אשך מבעי ליה דאין לחלק בין אדם לבהמה משום דבהמה יש לה שני כיסין וחשיב מום טפי דהא אפי' אין לו ביצים כלל (למעוטי) מבעי ליה למעוטי ממרוח אשך ושמא י"ל בכי האי גוונא שייך לומר דנשנה בשביל דבר שנתחדש בה כדר' ישמעאל דבסמוך וניחא נמי השתא אפי' יש מומין שנכתבו אע"ג דהוו נפקי ממום שבגלוי ואינו חוזר:
notes.en: In brief: The Gemara could equally have challenged from “cracked” [ḥarutz], which is not written of a person even though it applies to a person, in the gums and in the place of a bone, as in an animal. Likewise “crushed” and “cut” are not written of a person, and gibben is not written of an animal, even though it would apply to an animal according to the view below that a gibben is one whose spine is crooked, not one with unusual eyebrows. Tosafot then raise “no testicles, or only one,” which the mishna above (40a) counts as a blemish in an animal: that comes only from meroaḥ ashekh, as the first tanna later in this chapter calls it “the meroaḥ ashekh stated in the Torah,” and an animal is learned from a person by the verbal analogy just below. That works for the first tanna. But Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva need the verse for a missing testicle; from where do they know [the other case], which they themselves count as a blemish in the earlier chapter? If from “a visible blemish that does not return,” why would the first tanna need a verse for it? And they too would read the verse that way, were it not needed for the missing testicle. One cannot distinguish between a person and an animal on the grounds that an animal has two sacs, so the loss counts as more of a blemish, since even “no testicles at all” must be excluded from meroaḥ ashekh. Perhaps in such a case one may say that it was repeated for the new element it introduces, as the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches below; and this also explains why some blemishes are written even though they would follow from “a visible blemish that does not return.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.

notes.he: פוסלין באדם והא איכא יבלת דלא כתיבא באדם וכתיב בבהמה ודק תבלול דלא כתיבי באורייתא גבי מומי בהמה ואמאי קא חשיב להו הכא בבהמה:
notes.en: And why: do they disqualify in a person? But there is the wart, which is not written regarding a person and is written regarding an animal; and cataract and tevallul, which are not written in the Torah among the blemishes of an animal, so why does he count them here for an animal?

messages.text: And furthermore, there are also the blemishes of a cataract and a tevallul, which appear in the Torah with regard to a person but are not written in the Torah with regard to an animal (see Leviticus 21:20). Why, then, does the mishna on 38a teach that such blemishes disqualify an animal?

verse.he: אוֹ־גִבֵּן אוֹ־דַק אוֹ תְּבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ אוֹ גָרָב אוֹ יַלֶּפֶת אוֹ מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ׃
verse.en: or who is a hunchback, or a dwarf, or who has a growth in his eye, or who has a boil-scar, or scurvy, or crushed testes.

notes.he: דאמרן גבי מומי בכור הוא ולא כתיב בבהמה דבשלמא כולהו אינך דמנינן ביה כמו חוטין וזנב העגל שאינה מגעת לארכובה מכל מום רע נפקי אלא דק ותבלול איכא למיפרך מדגלינהו רחמנא באדם ובבהמה לא גלינהו ש"מ לא פסלי בבהמה. ומשני מילף ילפי מהדדי:
notes.en: And furthermore, cataract and tevallul: which we stated among the blemishes of the firstborn, yet they are not written regarding an animal. Granted, all the others we listed for it, such as the gums and a calf’s tail that does not reach the leg joint, come from “any ill blemish.” But cataract and tevallul can be challenged: since the Merciful One revealed them for a person and did not reveal them for an animal, learn from this that they do not disqualify in an animal. And he answers: they are derived from one another.

messages.text: These blemishes are derived from one another, as it is taught in a baraita:

notes.he: מומי בהמה ממומי אדם הלכך חשיב להו לכולהו בבהמה:
notes.en: They are derived from one another: the blemishes of an animal from the blemishes of a person; therefore he counts all of them for an animal.

messages.text: In the case of a person, i.e., a priest, it is not stated of him that a wart disqualifies him from Temple service, and in the case of an animal, it is not stated that a cataract or a tevallul disqualify it from being sacrificed. From where is it derived that one applies that which is said of this case to that case, and that which is said of this case to that case? The verse states: “Scabbed” and “scabbed,” “scurvy” and “scurvy,” both with regard to a person and an animal (Leviticus 21:20; 22:22), which serves to draw a verbal analogy from the verses.

notes.he: גרב ילפת כתיב בין במומי אדם בין במומי בהמה לגזרה שוה:
notes.en: Garav and yalefet are written both among the blemishes of a person and among the blemishes of an animal, for the verbal analogy.

messages.text: These verses must be free, i.e., they are superfluous and are stated only for the purpose of the verbal analogy. This means that the verbal analogy cannot be refuted by logical reasoning, whereas if the verses are not free one can refute the analogy if there is a significant difference between the two cases.

As, if they are not free, the verbal analogy can be refuted as follows: One cannot derive the disqualifications of a person for performing the Temple service from those of an animal, as the case of an animal can be considered more stringent because the animal itself is sacrificed upon the altar. Similarly, one cannot derive the disqualifications of an animal from those of a person, as one can claim that the halakha with regard to a person should be more stringent, since a person was included in the performance of mitzvot.
Indeed, the terms are free. Accordingly, since these disqualifications are derived from a verbal analogy they must be accepted as though they were written explicitly in the Torah.

Let the Merciful One write that scurvy disqualifies a person and an animal, and it would be unnecessary for the Merciful One to write that a scab disqualifies them, as I would say: And if scurvy, which is not repulsive, is considered a disqualifying blemish, then in the case of a scab, which is repulsive, is it not all the more so a disqualifying blemish? If so, then with regard to “scabbed” and “scabbed,” which the Merciful One writes with regard to a person and an animal, why do I need them? Evidently, they are to be considered free for the verbal analogy.

notes.he: מילפת דקשה הוא כחרס ומשקע בבשר ועושה חריצין:
notes.en: Garav, which is repulsive: more than yalefet, since it is hard as earthenware, sinks into the flesh and makes cracks.

notes.he: תימה הא איצטריך לכדאמר רבא בפירקין דלעיל (בכורות דף מא.) דלהכי כתב רחמנא גרב למימר דחרוץ במקום בשר לא הוי מומא ומיהו תרי גרב ותרי ילפת כתיבי חד באדם וחד בבהמה ואייתר חד לאפנויי אבל ע"כ לא הוי מופנה אלא מצד אחד ואיכא למ"ד ב"ק (דף כה:) דמשיבין ועוד דמדנקט בברייתא ת"ל גרב גרב ילפת ילפת ל"ל למעבד גזירה שוה בתרווייהו משמע דנקיט הכי משום דבכל הני תרי דוכתי כתיב גרב בהדי ילפת לאפנויי וי"ל דמשום דרשא דרבא דלעיל לא מפיק הפנאה מהכא כיון דלפי דרשא לא מיתוקמא גרב לגופיה אלא ללמד החרום במקום בשר:
notes.en: Garav, which the Merciful One wrote, why do I need it? [It is free]: This is puzzling, since it is needed for what Rava said in the previous chapter (41a): the Merciful One wrote garav to teach that a crack in the place of flesh is not a blemish. However, two garavs and two yalefets are written, one for a person and one for an animal, so one is left over to make it free. But then it is necessarily free on one side only, and there is an opinion in Bava Kamma (25b) that such an analogy can be refuted. Furthermore, since the baraita says, “The verse states: ‘scabbed’ and ‘scabbed,’ ‘scurvy’ and ‘scurvy,’” why does it need to draw the verbal analogy from both? This implies that it says so because in both places garav is written together with yalefet, to make it free. One may answer that Rava’s exposition above does not remove the freeing from here, since according to that exposition garav is not used for itself but only to teach about a crack [the printed text reads ḥarum, apparently for ḥarutz] in the place of flesh.

notes.he: ומה ילפת דלא מאיסא דהוי יבש:
notes.en: And if yalefet, which is not repulsive: since it is dry.

notes.he: דהוי לח:
notes.en: Garav, which is repulsive: since it is moist.

messages.text: But if animals and priests are disqualified by the same blemishes, let the Merciful One write all the disqualifying blemishes with regard to one of them, either a person or an animal, and let the Merciful One write that a scab and scurvy disqualify both here and here, for the purpose of the verbal analogy, and let all the other blemishes be derived in one case from the other one, through the verbal analogy.

notes.he: מומי או באדם או בבהמה:
notes.en: And let the Merciful One write them all: the blemishes, either for a person or for an animal.

notes.he: גרב לגזירה שוה וילפת לגלויי עלה דגרב דמופנה הוא אמאי כתב עור ופסח ושבור הכא והכא:
notes.en: And garav and yalefet here and here: garav for the verbal analogy, and yalefet to show that garav is free. [Otherwise,] why did He write blind, lame and broken both here and here?

notes.he: מומי בין יבלת בין דק תבלול בחד ולא באידך אלא גרב וילפת לחוד באידך למילף או גבי אדם או גבי בהמה:
notes.en: And let the Merciful One write all the blemishes, the wart as well as cataract and tevallul, in one and not in the other, and only garav and yalefet in the other, to derive [the rest], either regarding a person or regarding an animal.

messages.text: To which is this referring, i.e., in which case should the Merciful One write all the blemishes? If the Merciful One had written all of them with regard to a person then I would say: All blemishes that disqualify in the case of a person likewise disqualify in the case of an animal. If so, then with regard to closed hooves and damaged gums, which are not written with regard to a person as they are not relevant because a person has no hooves and his gums are covered with teeth, I would say: In the case of an animal as well they should not disqualify.

notes.he: בהי מינייהו לכתבינהו רחמנא דלילף אידך מיניה:
notes.en: Regarding which should He write: in which of them should the Merciful One write them, so that the other is derived from it?

notes.he: דאדם אינו מפריס פרסה ואינן נוהגין בו מומי חוטין דאדם יש לו שינים ואין נראין החוטין ובהמה הוא דאית לה שיניים למעלה ונראין החוטים ונפסלת בפגימתן:
notes.en: Closed hooves and gums, which do not exist in a person: for a person does not have parted hooves, and blemishes of the gums do not apply to him, since a person has teeth and the gums are not visible; whereas an animal has teeth above [so the printed text reads; cattle in fact have no upper front teeth, which is why the upper gum shows], and the gums are visible, and it is disqualified when they are damaged.

notes.he: להכי כתב רחמנא מומים בבהמה ומנה בה קלוט וחוטין שנפגמו ושנגממו דנפקי מחרוץ:
notes.en: In an animal too they should not disqualify: this is why the Merciful One wrote blemishes for an animal, and counted among them closed hooves and gums that were damaged or worn down, which come from “cracked” [ḥarutz].

notes.he: דחוטין דאדם לא הוי בגלוי כשל בהמה ולא פסלי באדם ולא קלוט דלא בעינן באדם פרסות סדוקות:
notes.en: Closed hooves and gums, which do not exist in a person: since a person’s gums are not exposed like an animal’s, they do not disqualify in a person; nor closed hooves, since we do not require split hooves in a person.

messages.text: And if you would say: Let the Merciful One write all the blemishes with regard to an animal, I would say: All blemishes that disqualify in the case of an animal likewise disqualify in the case of a person. Accordingly, with regard to a gibben, one with blemished eyebrows, or a ḥarum, one with a sunken nose, which are not written with regard to an animal as such blemishes do not occur among animals, I would say: In the case of a person as well they should not disqualify.

notes.he: דגבן היינו שיש לו גבינים שקורין שורציל"ש ובהמה לית לה גבינים וחרום היינו שחוטמו בין שתי עיניו ובהמה אין לה חוטם בין העינים:
notes.en: Gibben and ḥarum do not exist in an animal: a gibben is one who has [unusual] eyebrows [gevinim], called in Old French sourcils, and an animal has no eyebrows. A ḥarum is one whose nose [is sunken] between his two eyes, and an animal has no nose between the eyes.

notes.he: היינו לת"ק דלקמן בפירקין דמוקי גבן בגביני עינים אבל לרבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס דאמר שיש לו שני גבין ושני שדראות שייך שפיר בבהמה ולהכי לא קאמר נמי מרוח אשך דליתיה לר' חנינא בן אנטיגנוס דאמר כל שמראיו חשוכים דלא איירי אליביה:
notes.en: Gibben and ḥarum, which do not exist in an animal: this is according to the first tanna below in this chapter, who explains gibben as about the eyebrows. But according to Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, who says he has two backs and two spines, it applies well to an animal. And that is why it does not also list meroaḥ ashekh [among those that do not exist in an animal], which according to Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, who says it is anyone whose appearance is darkened, does not exist [in an animal]: because the Gemara here is not speaking according to him.

notes.he: גבן וחרום דליתנהו בבהמה דגיבן זה שגביניו שוכבין וליכא לבהמה גבינין:
notes.en: Gibben and ḥarum, which do not exist in an animal: for a gibben is one whose eyebrows lie [over his eyes], and an animal has no eyebrows.

notes.he: זה הכוחל שתי עיניו כאחת שחוטמו שקוע ואין לו חוטם בין עין לעין ויכול לכחול זה מזה שאין עיכוב חוטם בין עין לעין. וחוטם ליכא בבהמה ואינו כוחל:
notes.en: And ḥarum: this is one who paints both of his eyes as one, since his nose is sunken and he has no nose between eye and eye, so he can paint from one to the other, with no nose between the eyes to stop it. And an animal has no such nose and does not paint its eyes.

messages.text: Therefore, the Torah delineates all the disqualifying blemishes with regard to both an animal and a person in order to state the blemishes that are unique to animals and the blemishes that are unique to people.

But even so, why is it necessary for the Torah to delineate all the common blemishes? Let the Merciful One write all of them in the verses discussing one of them, either an animal or a person, and as for those that are not relevant for the other, i.e., those blemishes that apply only in the case of an animal, let the Merciful One write with regard to an animal, and as for those that are not relevant for the other, i.e., those blemishes relevant only to a person, let the Merciful One write with regard to a person.

notes.he: דלא שייכי ביה ליכתב באידך:
notes.en: And those that do not exist in the other: that are not relevant to it, let Him write them in the other.

notes.he: וליכתבינהו לכולהו מומי דשייכי בחד אי באדם ליכתוב ביה גיבן וחרום ולכולהו מומי:
notes.en: And let Him write all the blemishes that apply to one: if to a person, let Him write there gibben and ḥarum and all the blemishes.

messages.text: And let the Torah write the blemishes of a scab and scurvy both here and there, for the purpose of the verbal analogy, and let the fact that their common blemishes disqualify in both cases be derived from one another.

notes.he: ביה כגון קלוט וחוטין ליכתבינהו באידך בבהמה ולא ליכתוב בה תו מכל מומי אלא גרב וילפת. ולילפי מהדדי כל הני מומי דשייכי לכל חד וחד:
notes.en: And those that do not exist in it, such as closed hooves and gums, let Him write in the other, the animal, and not write there any more of the blemishes except garav and yalefet; and let all the blemishes that apply to each one be derived from one another.

messages.text: Rather, the reason the Torah repeats their common blemishes is in accordance with that which the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught,
Every passage in the Torah that was stated and repeated was repeated only for the novel element introduced therein.
messages.lead: as the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:

notes.he: והכא איכא חידוש באדם גבן וחרום ובבהמה קלוט וחוטין:
notes.en: That was introduced in it: and here there is something new in a person, gibben and ḥarum, and in an animal, closed hooves and gums.

messages.text: It is the style of the Torah to repeat a passage even in order to teach only one additional halakha. Consequently, with regard to the blemishes of a person and an animal, their common blemishes were repeated on account of those blemishes that apply only to an animal or a person.

notes.he: משום הכי איכתבו תרי זמני משום דבר שנתחדש בהן אגב דאיכא בהאי דליכא בהאי משום הכי כתבינהו תרי זימני:
notes.en: Rather: they were written twice because of the new element in them; since one has what the other does not, He wrote them twice.

messages.text: Why do I need the Merciful One to write that a blemish causes disqualification from Temple service in the case of a person, i.e., a priest (see Leviticus 21:17–23), and that a blemish causes disqualification in the case of sacrificial animals (see Leviticus 22:20–25), and that a blemish causes disqualification for sacrifice in the case of a firstborn animal (see Deuteronomy 15:21)?

verse.he: וְכִי־יִהְיֶה בוֹ מוּם פִּסֵּחַ אוֹ עִוֵּר כֹּל מוּם רָע לֹא תִזְבָּחֶנּוּ לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ׃
verse.en: But if it has a defect, lameness or blindness, any serious defect, you shall not sacrifice it to the ETERNAL your God.

notes.he: למיכתב דמומין פסולין באדם ומומין פסולין בבכור דכתיב (דברים ט״ו:כ״א) וכי יהיה בו מום וגו' ומומין פסולין בקדשים:
notes.en: Why do I need: to write that blemishes disqualify in a person, and that blemishes disqualify in a firstborn, as it is written, “And if there be any blemish therein” (Deuteronomy 15:21), and that blemishes disqualify in consecrated animals?

notes.dh: למה לי דכתב רחמנא מום באדם מום בבכור מום בקדשים צריכי כו'
notes.he: תימה למאי דקאמר צריכי דמשמע דלא ילפינן מהדדי מנלן באדם ובקדשים כל מום שבגלוי ואינו חוזר דגבי בכור הוא דדרשינן ליה לעיל בפרק על אלו מומין (בכורות דף לז.) מכלל ופרט וכן מומין דגבי אדם ובקדשים דלא כתיבי בבכור דאיכא דלא נפקי מכל מום רע כגון דק תבלול כדפי' בקונטרס בריש פירקין ויש לומר הואיל דגלי גלי:
notes.en: Why do I need that the Merciful One wrote a blemish in a person, a blemish in a firstborn, a blemish in consecrated animals? They are necessary, etc.: This is puzzling. Since it says “they are necessary,” which implies that we do not derive them from one another, from where do we know, for a person and for consecrated animals, every visible blemish that does not return, which for a firstborn we expound above in chapter Al Elu Mumin (37a) from a general rule and a detail? And likewise the blemishes of a person and of consecrated animals that are not written for a firstborn, some of which do not come from “any ill blemish,” such as cataract and tevallul, as Rashi explained at the beginning of this chapter. One may answer: since [the Torah] has revealed [that a blemish disqualifies in each case], it has revealed [that they share the same blemishes].

messages.text: They are all necessary. As, had the Merciful One written only that a blemish causes disqualification in the case of a person, one might suggest that blemishes cause disqualification only in that case, since a person was included in the performance of mitzvot.

notes.he: אדם כהן שכן נתרבה במצות הרבה מה שאין כן לא בבכור ולא בקדשים:
notes.en: A person, a priest, since he was included in many commandments, which is not so of a firstborn or of consecrated animals.

messages.text: Similarly, had the Merciful One written only that blemishes disqualify a firstborn animal from being sacrificed, it could be claimed that one cannot derive the disqualification of a person on account of blemishes from the disqualification of a firstborn animal, since an animal has an added aspect of stringency in that it itself is sacrificed upon the altar.

notes.he: כלומר אי כתב בבכור ולא כתב בהנך אדם מבכור לא אתי מה לבכור דין הוא שיפסלנו המום שכן הוא עצמו קרב:
notes.en: A person cannot be derived from a firstborn: that is, had He written it of a firstborn and not of these, a person could not be derived from a firstborn: what of a firstborn? It is fitting that a blemish disqualifies it, since it itself is offered.

messages.text: Additionally, one cannot derive the disqualifications of sacrificial animals from those of a firstborn animal, since the sanctity of a firstborn animal is from the womb, i.e., from birth, whereas the sanctity of other offerings applies only upon consecration by a person, and they are therefore of a lesser sanctity.

Furthermore, had the Merciful One written only that sacrificial animals are disqualified due to blemishes, it could be claimed that one cannot derive the disqualifications of a person from that of sacrificial animals, as the offerings themselves are sacrificed.

notes.he: כלומר אי כתב בקדשים ולא כתב בהנך הנך לא אתו מינייהו:
notes.en: A person cannot be derived from consecrated animals: that is, had He written it of consecrated animals and not of these, these could not be derived from them.

messages.text: Similarly, one cannot derive the disqualifications of a firstborn animal from those of sacrificial animals, as the sanctity of other offerings is greater than that of a firstborn animal because there are many types of other offerings, whereas a firstborn animal has only one type of sanctification. Therefore, it was necessary for the Merciful One to specify that blemishes disqualify in each case.

notes.he: שכן קדושתן מרובה שקדשים נוהגין בין בזכרים בין בנקבות ועוד שיש להן קדושת הרבה חטאת ואשם עולה ושלמים:
notes.en: Since their sanctity is greater: for consecrated animals apply to males and females alike, and furthermore they have many sanctities: sin offering and guilt offering, burnt offering and peace offering.

messages.text: Granted, the disqualification of one of these cases cannot be derived from only a single other one. But let one of them be derived from the other two.
messages.quote: a blemish in the case of a person … sacrificial animals … a firstborn

messages.text: From which two should the other one be derived? If you will say: Let the Merciful One not write that blemishes disqualify a firstborn animal and one should derive that case from these, i.e., the disqualifications of a person and sacrificial animals, this suggestion can be rejected. What is notable about these? They are notable in that their sanctity is greater than that of a firstborn offering, as in the case of a person, he is included in the performance of mitzvot; and in the case of a sacrificial animal, there are many types of offerings. Moreover, the halakhot of these blemishes apply to regular, i.e., non-firstborn, animals and people.

notes.he: חטאות ואשמות עולות ושלמים אדם קדושתו מרובה במצות:
notes.en: Their sanctity is great: [consecrated animals, with their many kinds:] sin offerings and guilt offerings, burnt offerings and peace offerings; a person, whose sanctity is great in commandments.

notes.he: מה להנך בקדשים ואדם קדושתו מרובה אדם נתרבה במצות קדשים שכן קדושתן מרובה ונוהג קדושת אדם כהן וקדשים בין בפשוטים בין בבכורים ראוין לעבודה:
notes.en: What of these, consecrated animals and a person, whose sanctity is great: a person was included in commandments, and consecrated animals, since their sanctity is great. And the sanctity of a person, a priest, and of consecrated animals applies to ordinary ones and firstborn alike, being fit for the service.

messages.text: Furthermore, if one will say: Let the Merciful One not write that blemishes disqualify sacrificial animals and one should derive that case from these cases, a person, i.e., a priest, and a firstborn animal, this too can be rejected: What is notable about these? They are notable in that their sanctity is automatic and requires no consecration, as a priest is a priest by virtue of being the son of a priest, and a firstborn attains its status by being the first child of its mother, while offerings are consecrated by their owners.

notes.he: קדושתן מאליהן שאין צריך להקדישן:
notes.en: Their sanctity is automatic: they need not be consecrated.

messages.text: Finally, if one will say: Let the Merciful One not write that blemishes disqualify a person and one should derive that case from these cases, the firstborn animal and sacrificial animals, this suggestion too can be rejected: What is notable about these? They are notable in that they themselves are sacrificed upon the altar, whereas a person is not. Therefore, all three verses are necessary, to teach that blemishes disqualify in all these cases.

notes.he: לא ליכתוב באדם ותיתי מהנך מבכור ומקדשים ואי אמרת מה לבכור שכן קדושתו מרחם תאמר באדם קדשים יוכיחו שאין קדוש מרחם ואפי' כן פוסל מום בהם. מה לקדשים שכן קדושתו מרובה בכור יוכיח וחזר הדין הצד השוה שבהן שפוסל בהן מום אף באדם נמי. מה להנך שכן קריבין על גבי מזבח מה שאין כן באדם:
notes.en: Let Him not write it of a person, and let it come from these, from a firstborn and from consecrated animals. And if you say: what of a firstborn, whose sanctity is from the womb, will you say so of a person? Consecrated animals prove it, for they are not sacred from the womb and even so a blemish disqualifies them. What of consecrated animals, whose sanctity is great? A firstborn proves it. And the argument comes back around: the feature common to them is that a blemish disqualifies them, so too a person. [The answer:] what of these, which are offered upon the altar, which is not so of a person?

messages.caption: Rava: priest, offerings and firstborn each have something the others lack, so the Torah must state the blemish law for each.

messages.text: The mishna teaches that in addition to those blemishes that disqualify an animal, there are other blemishes that apply to a person despite the fact that they are not actual defects. From where are these matters derived?
messages.quote: And in addition to those blemishes

messages.text: These halakhot are derived from that which the verse states: “No man among the seed of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come forward to sacrifice the offerings of the Lord made by fire” (Leviticus 21:21). The verse indicates that the priest must be a man who is equal among the seed of Aaron, i.e., one whose appearance is similar to the other priests.

verse.he: כׇּל־אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ מוּם מִזֶּרַע אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן לֹא יִגַּשׁ לְהַקְרִיב אֶת־אִשֵּׁי יְהֹוָה מוּם בּוֹ אֵת לֶחֶם אֱלֹהָיו לֹא יִגַּשׁ לְהַקְרִיב׃
verse.en: No man among the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a defect shall be qualified to offer GOD’s offering by fire; having a defect, he shall not be qualified to offer the food of his God.

notes.he: הוא דבעי מומא הא אין שוה בזרעו של אהרן בלא מומא נמי מיפסיל:
notes.en: A man who is equal among the seed of Aaron: it is he who needs a blemish [to be disqualified]; but one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron is disqualified even without a blemish.

notes.he: לא פסילי מדאורייתא אלא משום דבעינן איש ששוה בזרעו של אהרן:
notes.en: In addition to them in a person, the kilon, etc.: these are not disqualified by Torah law [as blemishes], but because we require a man who is equal among the seed of Aaron.

messages.text: What difference is there between a priest disqualified from performing the Temple service due to a full-fledged blemish that disqualifies both people and animals, and a priest disqualified from performing the Temple service because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron?
messages.quote: a man who is equal among the seed of Aaron

notes.he: בין כהן הנפסל במום גמור לכהן הנפסל משום שאין שוה בזרעו של אהרן דהיינו כילון וליפתן וכל הנך:
notes.en: What is there: between a priest disqualified by a full blemish and a priest disqualified because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron, that is, the kilon, the lifta and all those.

messages.text: There is a difference between them with regard to profaning the Temple service. A priest with a full-fledged blemish who performs rites in the Temple profanes the service he has performed, as it is written: “He has a blemish; that he not profane My Sanctuaries” (Leviticus 21:23). A priest who is not equal among the seed of Aaron does not profane the service he performs.

verse.he: אַךְ אֶל־הַפָּרֹכֶת לֹא יָבֹא וְאֶל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ לֹא יִגַּשׁ כִּי־מוּם בּוֹ וְלֹא יְחַלֵּל אֶת־מִקְדָּשַׁי כִּי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה מְקַדְּשָׁם׃
verse.en: but he shall not enter behind the curtain or come near the altar, for he has a defect. He shall not profane these places sacred to Me, for I GOD have sanctified them.

messages.text: What difference is there between a priest disqualified from performing the Temple service because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron, e.g., one whose head is pointed, and a priest disqualified from performing the Temple service due to the mere appearance of a blemish, such as one whose eyelashes have fallen out, as stated in the mishnayot further on in this chapter?

notes.he: כגון הנך דקחשיב במתני' משום מראית העין שמאוסין לראות כגון שנשרו ריסי עיניו ושנטלו שיניו:
notes.en: Because of appearance: such as those the mishna lists “because of appearance,” who are unpleasant to look at, such as one whose eyelashes fell out and one whose teeth were removed.

notes.dh: מאי איכא בין שאין שוה לזרעו ומשום מראית העין
notes.he: דמשום מראית העין הוי קיל מכולהו:
notes.en: What is there between one who is not equal among his seed and “because of appearance”: for “because of appearance” is more lenient than all of them.

messages.text: There is a difference between them with regard to the violation of the prohibition, which is stated as a positive mitzva, i.e., that priests who are equal shall serve in the Temple. A priest who is not equal among the seed of Aaron who performs the Temple service transgresses this prohibition. By contrast, a priest who is disqualified due to the appearance of a blemish is disqualified by rabbinic law, and he does not transgress a Torah prohibition by performing the Temple service.

notes.he: מי שאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן עובר בעשה אם עבד דהכי משמע השוה בזרע אהרן הוי כהן ויעבוד שאינו שוה לא יעבוד ולאו הבא מכלל עשה עשה:
notes.en: A positive commandment: one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron transgresses a positive commandment if he served, for this is the implication: one who is equal among the seed of Aaron is a priest and shall serve; one who is not equal shall not serve. And a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive commandment has the status of a positive commandment.

notes.he: דכתיב מזרע אהרן הכהן מי ששוה בזרעו של אהרן ראוי לעבודה ושאינו שוה אין ראוי לעבודה והיינו לאו הבא מכלל עשה עשה. למראית העין אפילו איסור עשה ליכא:
notes.en: There is a positive commandment between them: as it is written, “of the seed of Aaron the priest”: one who is equal among the seed of Aaron is fit for the service, and one who is not equal is not fit; and this is a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive commandment, which has the status of a positive commandment. For “appearance” there is not even the prohibition of a positive commandment.

messages.caption: Three levels of disqualification for a priest, and what each one means if he serves anyway.

messages.text: One whose head is pointed [kilon], this is one whose head resembles the cover of a barrel, narrow above and wide below.
messages.quote: One whose head is pointed … turnip-like

notes.he: לכסוי של חבית (מלמעלה) שחד מלמעלה ורחב מלמטה וחבירו בסנהדרין בפ' זה בורר לו אחד (דף כח:) כי אכלא לדנא:
notes.en: Like a cover [akhla]: like the cover of a barrel, which is narrow above and wide below. Its parallel is in Sanhedrin, chapter Zeh Borer (28b): “like a cover for a barrel.”

notes.he: לאכלא דדנא שהוא משופע וחד למעלה:
notes.en: The kilon: like the lid of a barrel, which slopes and is narrow at the top.

messages.text: One whose head is turnip-like, this is one whose head resembles the top of a turnip, wide above and narrow below.

notes.he: לראש הלפת שראשה רחב והולכת וכלה למטה:
notes.en: Like the top of a turnip: the head of the turnip, which is wide and narrows as it goes down.

notes.he: שדומה ראשו ללפת שרחב למעלה מכל צדדין:
notes.en: Lifta: his head resembles a turnip, which is wide at the top on all sides.

messages.text: And his neck stands in the middle of his head, i.e., his head protrudes equally in all directions around his neck, whereas a typical person’s neck is situated at the back of his head.
messages.lead: The Sages taught in a baraita another detail relating to this blemish:

notes.he: שראשו בולט לאחוריו כלפניו:
notes.en: In the middle of the head: his head protrudes behind as much as in front.

notes.he: כגון שצוארו עומד באמצע ראשו שהראש בולט מכל סביביו. מקבא. דדמי ראשיה למקבא שבולט הפדחת הרבה לחוץ וכן העורף מאחריו ולצדעיו שוה ראשו ודומה לפטיש שיוצא מלפניו ומלאחריו והיינו מקבא כגון ותשם את המקבת בידה:
notes.en: And it was taught: for example, his neck stands in the middle of his head, so that the head protrudes on all sides. Makkava: his head resembles a hammer, for the forehead protrudes far forward, and likewise the nape behind, while at the temples his head is even; it resembles a hammer that projects in front and behind. This is makkava, as in “and she took the hammer [makkevet] in her hand” (Judges 4:21).

messages.text: One whose head is hammer-like [makkavan], this is one whose head resembles a hammer, with his forehead protruding.

notes.he: לקרדום שערפו עגול וקצר ברוחב:
notes.en: Like a makkava: like an axe, whose back is rounded and short in width.

messages.text: And one whose head is indented [shakut], this is one with a depression in the front of his head.

notes.he: שראשו משופע מלפניו באלכסון כעין כלי של נגר שקורין בשגו"ג:
notes.en: Shakut in front: his head slopes diagonally in front, like a carpenter’s tool (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: שראשו בולט הרבה לפניו:
notes.en: Shakut in front: his head protrudes greatly in front.

messages.text: And one wherein the back of his head protrudes [sekifat] is someone for whom it appears a piece from the back of his head has been removed, as people say: A piece has been taken [shakil pisa]. Sekifat is understood to be an abbreviation of that term.

notes.he: שגובה ראשו חסר מאחוריו:
notes.en: Behind: the height of his head is lacking at the back.

notes.he: שנראה כמי שניטל ממנו חתיכה:
notes.en: Shakil pisa: he looks like one from whom a piece has been taken.

notes.he: שדומה כמי שנחתך ממנו חתיכה מאחריו והיינו שקיל פיסיא:
notes.en: And sekifa behind: he looks like one from whom a piece was cut at the back; and this is shakil pisa.

messages.text: And a priest whose neck is short, or one whose neck is narrow, is disqualified from performing the Temple service as well.
A priest with a short neck is one whose neck is hidden and is not visible between his shoulders. A priest with a narrow neck is one whose neck is long and narrow.

notes.he: שראשו מוטל בין כתפיו ודומה כמי שראשו שמוט אשלויישו"ד:
notes.en: Ḥavi miḥba [hidden]: his head rests between his shoulders, and he looks like one whose head has sunk down (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). [Rashi’s text reads ḥavi miḥba, “hidden,” as the Davidson English translates; the printed Gemara reads ḥavis miḥbas, “pressed in.”]

notes.he: שצוארו משוקע בין כתיפיו ושמוט דאריך צוארו ודק ובולט פרצופו הרבה לחוץ:
notes.en: Ḥavis miḥbas [pressed in]: his neck is sunk between his shoulders. And shamut [drawn out]: his neck is long and thin, and his face juts far forward.

messages.text: In a case where there is a bone in his hump, everyone agrees that the priest is disqualified for Temple service. They disagree when there is no bone.
messages.quote: those with humped backs, Rabbi Yehuda deems them fit

notes.he: שלועזין חלדרובא:
notes.en: Those with humps: which they call in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss).

messages.text: One Sage, i.e., the Rabbis, holds that this person is not equal among the seed of Aaron and is therefore disqualified from performing the Temple service; and one Sage, Rabbi Yehuda, holds that it is merely a piece of flesh and is not considered a blemish.

notes.he: חתיכה:
notes.en: Karkura: a piece.

notes.he: היינו תלתול בעלמא:
notes.en: A piece of flesh [karkura]: this is merely a lump.

messages.text: The Sages taught that a kere’aḥ is disqualified only if he does not have a row of hair in the back of his head but he has a row of hair in the front. But if he has a row of hair both in the front and in the back, he is fit for performing the Temple service. And all the more so, when he has hair in the back but he does not have in the front he is fit for performing the Temple service, as this is typical of older men.

notes.he: שיטה של שער מקפת מאזן לאזן לאחריו ויש לו לפניו:
notes.en: They taught only where he does not have: a row of hair encircling from ear to ear at the back, but has one in front.

notes.dh: אבל יש לו לאחריו ולפניו כשר וכל שכן שיש לו לאחריו ואין לו לפניו
notes.he: דטפי הוי נוי בשיש לו לאחריו ולא לפניו יותר מכשיש לו סביב כל הראש ובאמצע הוי קרח:
notes.en: But if he has it at the back and in front he is fit, and all the more so if he has it at the back and not in front: since it is more becoming when he has it at the back and not in front than when he has it all around the head and is bald in the middle.

notes.he: יש גירסא אחרת בספרים לבד גירסת הקונטרס:
notes.en: Rava said: they taught only, etc.: there is another reading in the books besides the reading of the Kuntres [Rashi].

messages.text: The Sages taught that such a person is fit only when he has a row of hair in the back but he does not have in the front. But if he has a row of hair both in the back and in the front, he is disqualified from performing the Temple service. And all the more so, one who has a row of hair in the front and does not have in the back, or one who does not have any hair at all, is disqualified.
messages.lead: And there are those who teach the statement of Rava with regard to the latter clause of the mishna: And if he has a row of hair, that person is fit for performing the Temple service.
messages.quote: If he has a row of hair from ear to ear, that person is fit

notes.he: דמתני' לא שנו דיש לו כשר אלא שיש לו לאחריו שיטה מקפת מאזן לאזן ולא לפניו אבל יש לו נמי לפניו פסול וכ"ש שאין לו כלל:
notes.en: And some teach it on the latter clause: the mishna’s “if he has, he is fit” was taught only where he has a row encircling from ear to ear at the back and not in front; but if he has one in front as well, he is disqualified, and all the more so if he has none at all.

messages.text: The bald priests, and the priests who are dwarves, and the priests with leaky eyes, are disqualified from performing the Temple service, since they are not equal among the seed of Aaron.

notes.he: שעיניהם זבות וזולגות מים:
notes.en: Zavlegan: whose eyes run and drip water.

notes.he: איכא דאמרי שיש לפלוף בעינו. וא"ד שיוצא רירו:
notes.en: And the zavlegan: some say he has rheum in his eye, and some say a discharge comes out of it.

messages.text: Why is it necessary for Rabbi Yoḥanan to state this? With regard to bald priests, we learn in the mishna that they are disqualified. Similarly, with regard to priests who are dwarves, we learn in a mishna (45b) that they are disqualified.
messages.quote: The bald priests, and the priests who are dwarves

notes.he: במתני' הקפח והננסין והחרש:
notes.en: Dwarves, we learned: in the mishna (45b): “the kipe’aḥ, the dwarves and the deaf.”

notes.he: קרחנין וננסין תנינא במתניתא ומאי קמ"ל ולשמעינן זבלגנין גרידא:
notes.en: The bald and the dwarves we learned in the mishna, so what does he teach us? Let him teach us the zavlegan alone.

messages.text: It was necessary for him to teach us this statement with regard to priests with leaky eyes, as the halakha with regard to them does not appear in any mishna.

notes.he: דלא תנן:
notes.en: It was necessary for him [to teach] the zavlegan: which we did not learn [in a mishna].

messages.text: And furthermore, it was necessary for him to reiterate the halakha with regard to bald priests and dwarves lest you say they are disqualified only by rabbinic law, due to the appearance of a blemish. Rabbi Yoḥanan therefore teaches that they are disqualified by Torah law, as they are not equal among the seed of Aaron.

notes.he: כלומר והנך נמי איצטריכו דמהו דתימא הא דפסיל להו במתניתין משום מראית העין פסיל להו ולא עברו בעשה אי פלחי להכי אשמעינן רבי יוחנן דמשום שאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן:
notes.en: And lest you say, etc.: that is, these too were necessary. For lest you say that the mishna disqualifies them because of appearance, and they do not transgress a positive commandment if they serve, Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that it is because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron.

notes.he: כולהו איצטריך ליה דמהו דתימא משום מראית העין נינהו קמ"ל משום דשאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן:
notes.en: He needed all of them, for lest you say they are disqualified because of appearance, he teaches us that it is because he is not equal among the seed of Aaron.

messages.text: But anywhere that a priest is deemed disqualified due to the appearance of a blemish, the tanna teaches this explicitly, e.g., in the mishna on this amud: And one whose eyelashes have fallen out is disqualified from performing the Temple service, due to the appearance of a blemish.

notes.he: שערו שבבבת העין:
notes.en: The eyelashes: the hairs at the eye.

notes.he: ואמאי מספקא לן דמשום מראית העין:
notes.en: And why would we be uncertain whether it is because of appearance? [The tanna states that reason wherever it applies.]

messages.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement is necessary, lest you say the tanna taught explicitly in one instance that a priest is disqualified due to the appearance of a blemish but the same is true with regard to all of those listed after the first clause of the mishna, starting from the case of priests with humped backs. Therefore, Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches that this is not the halakha.

notes.he: מבעלי חטרות ואילך דסד"א הא דאפיקנא ממי שאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן לעיל לא קאי אלא אכילון וליפתן ומקבן והנך דבבא קמייתא:
notes.en: And the same applies to all of them: from those with humps onward. For one might think that what we derived above from “one who is not equal among the seed of Aaron” refers only to the kilon, the lifta, the makkavan and those of the first clause.

notes.he: משום מראית העין וה"ה לכולהו להכי קמ"ל ר' יוחנן דמשום דאינו שוה הוא:
notes.en: Lest you say: he taught one case “because of appearance,” and the same applies to all of them; therefore Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that it is because he is not equal.

messages.text: But anywhere that there is a priest disqualified due to the appearance of a blemish, the tanna repeats and teaches explicitly that this is the reason. As the tanna repeats and teaches (44a): And one whose teeth fell out is disqualified due to the appearance of a blemish.

notes.he: והא כל היכא דאיכא אחריתי משום מראית העין הדר תני ליה דקתני סיפא ושניטלו שיניו כו' - ומההיא ידענא דרישא דתנא מראית העין לא קאי אלא אנשרו ריסי עיניו דאי אכולהו קאי למה ליה למיהדר ומיתנא. אלא הא דאתא ר' יוחנן:
notes.en: But wherever there is another case of “because of appearance,” he repeats it, as he teaches in the latter clause, “and one whose teeth were removed…”: from that I know that in the first clause, where he taught “appearance,” it refers only to one whose eyelashes fell out; for if it referred to all of them, why would he need to repeat it? So why did Rabbi Yoḥanan come [to teach this]?

notes.he: והיכי מצי למימר תני חדא וה"ה לכולהו והא כל היכא דאיכא למיהדר ומיתנא משום מראית העין קא הדר ותני מלמד דלא אמרינן תנא חדא וה"ה לכולהו. ומאי קמ"ל ר' יוחנן:
notes.en: And how can he say “he taught one and the same applies to all,” when wherever he can repeat and teach “because of appearance,” he repeats and teaches it? This shows that we do not say “he taught one and the same applies to all.” So what does Rabbi Yoḥanan teach us?

messages.text: Rather, the reason Rabbi Yoḥanan reiterates the halakha with regard to a bald priest and a dwarf is to exclude that which is taught in a baraita, as it is taught in a baraita:

notes.he: דלא פסיל להו אלא משום מראית העין וקמ"ל רבי יוחנן דהלכתא כמתניתין דפסלא להו משום דאין שוין בזרעו של אהרן:
notes.en: He came to exclude this tanna: who disqualifies them only because of appearance. Rabbi Yoḥanan teaches us that the halakha follows the mishna, which disqualifies them because they are not equal among the seed of Aaron.

notes.he: אלא הא קמ"ל לאפוקי מהאי תנא כו':
notes.en: Rather, this is what he teaches us: to exclude this tanna, etc.

messages.text: The bald priests, the dwarves, and the priests with leaky eyes are fit for performing the Temple service by Torah law, and the Sages said they are disqualified only due to the appearance of a blemish.
Rabbi Yoḥanan therefore teaches that they are disqualified by Torah law, as they are not equal among the seed of Aaron.
Who is this tanna who says that such priests are fit by Torah law? It is Rabbi Yehuda, as it is taught in a baraita that
messages.quote: are fit for performing the Temple service by Torah law

messages.text: When the verse states: “And Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall lay the pieces” (Leviticus 1:8), this serves to include the bald priests in the performance of the Temple service.

verse.he: וְעָרְכוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים אֵת הַנְּתָחִים אֶת־הָרֹאשׁ וְאֶת־הַפָּדֶר עַל־הָעֵצִים אֲשֶׁר עַל־הָאֵשׁ אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ׃
verse.en: and Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall lay out the sections, with the head and the suet, on the wood that is on the fire upon the altar.

notes.he: וערכו בני אהרן הכהנים (ויקרא א׳:ח׳):
notes.en: The priests: “And Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall lay…” (Leviticus 1:8).

notes.he: שכשרים לעבודה. על פסוק זה מצאתיה בתורת כהנים:
notes.en: To include the bald: that they are fit for the service. I found it on this verse in Torat Kohanim.

notes.he: והקריבו בני אהרן ואמאי כתיב הכהנים לרבות את הקרחנין:
notes.en: The priests: “and Aaron’s sons shall offer”; why then is “the priests” written? To include the bald.

messages.text: Mishna
If a priest has no eyebrows, or if he has only one eyebrow, that is the gibben that is stated in the Torah in the list of blemished priests (see Leviticus 21:20).

notes.he: שורציל"ש:
notes.en: Mishna. Eyebrows [gevinim]: in Old French, sourcils.

notes.he: גבות עינים:
notes.en: He has no gevinin: eyebrows.

messages.text: A gibben is one whose eyebrows are so long that they lie flat and cover his eyes.

notes.he: ששערות גביניו גדולים ומוטלין על פניו:
notes.en: Whose eyebrows lie: the hairs of his eyebrows are long and lie over his face.

notes.he: שהן גדולות ותלויות על עיניו:
notes.en: Anyone whose eyebrows lie: which are large and hang over his eyes.

messages.text: A gibben is one who has two backs and two spines.
Gemara
But does gibben mean one who does not have eyebrows? And the Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita:
messages.quote: that is the gibben that is stated in the Torah

messages.text: When it is stated that a priest who is a gibben is disqualified from performing the Temple service (see Leviticus 21:20), this is referring to one who has many eyebrows. With regard to one who has no eyebrows or who has only one eyebrow, from where is it derived that he is disqualified as well? The same verse states: “Or a gibben.”

verse.he: אוֹ־גִבֵּן אוֹ־דַק אוֹ תְּבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ אוֹ גָרָב אוֹ יַלֶּפֶת אוֹ מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ׃
verse.en: or who is a hunchback, or a dwarf, or who has a growth in his eye, or who has a boil-scar, or scurvy, or crushed testes.

notes.he: ששני גבות עיניו מצטרפות ואין הפרש חלק בין זו לזו:
notes.en: Gemara. Many eyebrows: his two eyebrows join, with no smooth space between one and the other.

messages.text: Clearly, the disqualification of one lacking eyebrows is not derived from the mention of a gibben, but from the term “or.”
The mishna should be understood as follows: One who has no eyebrows is disqualified, and this is derived from the exposition of the phrase “or a gibben.”

notes.he: והכי קאמר זהו או גבן האמור בתורה (ויקרא כא). ור' דוסא פליג עליה ולא דריש או:
notes.en: This is the exposition of “or a gibben”: this is what it means: this is the “or a gibben” stated in the Torah (Leviticus 21). And Rabbi Dosa disagrees with him and does not expound “or.”

notes.he: רבא אמר זהו גיבן האמור בתורה דקאמר זהו מדרש או גבן האמור בתורה כלומר דמאו מרבי אין לו אלא גבין אחד:
notes.en: Rava said: “This is the gibben stated in the Torah” means: this is the exposition of “or a gibben” stated in the Torah; that is, from “or” it includes one who has only one eyebrow.

messages.text: Is this to say that a person with two backs and two spines is capable of living? But it was stated that the Sages discussed the case of one who miscarries an entity that has two backs and two spines,
messages.lead: The mishna teaches that Rabbi Dosa says a gibben is one whose eyebrows are so long that they lie flat and cover his eyes, and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus says that a gibben is one who has two backs and two spines.
messages.quote: who has two backs and two spines

notes.he: מי שיש לו ב' גבין ושתי שדראות דפסיל ר' חנינא בן אנטיגנוס:
notes.en: That is to say it lives: one who has two backs and two spines, whom Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus disqualifies.

messages.text: In the case of a woman who miscarries such an entity, it is not considered an offspring, as it cannot survive, and therefore she does not have the ritual impurity caused by childbirth, and in the case of an animal who miscarries, the entity is prohibited for consumption.

notes.he: ואינה טמאה לידה:
notes.en: It is not an offspring: and she does not have the impurity of childbirth.

notes.he: כנבילה דנפל הוא וכמת דמי ולא מהניא ליה שחיטה:
notes.en: Prohibited for consumption: like a carcass, since it is a nonviable birth and is considered dead, and slaughter does not help it.

notes.he: פי' בקונטרס דלא מהני ליה שחיטה מטעם נפל משמע דאיירי כשיצא לאויר העולם ואי אפשר לומר כן דבפ' המפלת (נדה דף כד.) מוקי לה בנמצא במעי אמו דלא מישתרי לרב בשחיטת אמו ושמואל פליג עליה התם ושרי ליה בשחיטת אמו אבל ביצא לאויר אסור אפילו לשמואל ופריך רב שימי התם ממתני' דהכא ופירש שם בקונטרס אתרוייהו פריך לרב ושמואל דהך ר' חנינא בן אנטיגנוס גבי מומי בהמה מתניא ומיפסל ליה לגבוה מכלל דלהדיוט שרי והקשה עליו ר"ת דבהדיא תני ליה הכא גבי מומי אדם אלא לרב דוקא פריך דאמר באשה אינו ולד [אלמא] דלא חיי ומדפסל ליה הכא לעבודה מכלל דחיי וכן משמע דלרב דוקא פריך:
notes.en: In an animal it is prohibited for consumption: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that slaughter does not help it because it is a nonviable birth, which implies that it speaks of one that came out into the air of the world. That cannot be said, since in chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 24a) it is set where it was found inside its mother, and Rav does not permit it through its mother’s slaughter, while Shmuel disagrees there and permits it through its mother’s slaughter; but if it came out into the air, it is prohibited even according to Shmuel. Rav Shimi raises his difficulty there from our mishna here, and there the Kuntres explained that he challenges both Rav and Shmuel, since this teaching of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus is taught among the blemishes of animals and disqualifies it for the altar, implying it is permitted for ordinary eating. Rabbeinu Tam challenged him, since here it is explicitly taught among the blemishes of a person. Rather, he challenges Rav alone, who says that in a woman it is not an offspring, so evidently it does not live; and since here it is disqualified from the service, evidently it lives. And so too the passage implies that he challenges only Rav.

notes.he: דלא חיי:
notes.en: In a woman it is not an offspring: since it does not live.

messages.text: Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya already raised this contradiction to Rav, his grandfather,

notes.he: במסכת נדה:
notes.en: Already raised it to him: in Tractate Niddah.

messages.text: @Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya Are you really Shimi? Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus is not referring literally to someone with two backs and two spines, but to a person whose spine is crooked, causing it to appear as though he has two spines. Such a person can survive but is disqualified from performing the Temple service.

notes.he: חכם גדול כמותך אינו יודע לתרץ מתני' דמשמע חיי לאו בשני גבנין ממש קאמר אלא ששדרתו עקומה ומיחזי כגבין ושדראות הרבה וכי קאמינא אנא בשני גבין ממש:
notes.en: Are you Shimi?: does a great scholar like you not know how to resolve the mishna? The mishna implies that he lives, so it does not mean literally two backs, but one whose spine is crooked and looks like many backs and spines; and when I spoke, I meant literally two backs.

notes.he: והיינו דקאמר ר' חנניה כל שיש בו ב' גבין וב' שדרות הוי מום אבל ב' שדרות ממש לא:
notes.en: Where his spine is crooked, so that it looks like two spines. This is what Rabbi Ḥananya [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the mishna reads Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus] meant: anyone with two backs and two spines has a blemish; but not literally two spines.

messages.text: Mishna
The ḥarum is disqualified from performing the Temple service. What is a ḥarum? It is one who can paint both of his eyes as one, with one brushstroke, because he has a sunken nose.

notes.he: שאין לו כלל חוטם בין שתי עיניו וכשהוא כוחל עיניו במכחול יכול למשוך המכחול מעין לעין ואין החוטם מעכבו:
notes.en: Mishna. One who paints both of his eyes as one: he has no nose at all between his two eyes, so when he paints his eyes with the kohl stick he can draw the stick from eye to eye, and the nose does not stop it.

messages.text: If both of one’s eyes are above or both of his eyes are below; or if one of his eyes is above and one of his eyes is below; or if both eyes are in the proper place but he sees both the room on the ground floor and the upper story as one, at the same time;

notes.he: כדמפרש בגמרא:
notes.en: Both of his eyes above: as explained in the Gemara.

messages.text: and likewise those unable to look at the sun; and one whose eyes are different; and one whose eyes tear constantly, these are disqualified from performing the Temple service.

notes.he: שאינו יכול להסתכל כנגד החמה:
notes.en: Sekhei shemesh: who cannot look toward the sun.

notes.he: מפרש בגמ':
notes.en: The zagdan and the tzairan: explained in the Gemara.

notes.he: מפרש בגמרא סני שמש כדפי' בקונטרס ששונא את השמש ואינו יכול לראות מקום שהחמה זורחת שם וסכי הוא לשון חסוכי שמש שנמנע ממנו אור השמש:
notes.en: Sekhei shemesh: the Gemara explains it as sanei shemesh, as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: one who hates the sun and cannot look at a place where the sun shines. And sekhei means ḥasukhei shemesh, those from whom the sunlight is withheld.

messages.text: And one whose eyelashes have fallen out is disqualified from performing the Temple service due to the appearance of a blemish. Unlike the others listed in this mishna, who are disqualified by Torah law, one with this condition is not disqualified by Torah law. Rather, the Sages issued a decree prohibiting a priest with such a condition to perform the Temple service.

notes.he: שערות שבבבת עיניו:
notes.en: His eyelashes: the hairs at the eye.

notes.he: אנשרו ריסי עיניו קאי:
notes.en: Because of appearance: this refers to one whose eyelashes fell out.

notes.he: משמע שקורא ריס לשערות שרגילים להיות נושרין מרוב דמעה כי ההוא דרבן גמליאל בחלק (סנהדרין דף קד:) גבי בכה תבכה וזימנין דקרי ריס עור המקיף את העין כי ההוא דפרקין דלעיל (בכורות דף לח.) ריס שנקב ושנסדק ומפרש תורא ברא דעיניה:
notes.en: And one whose eyelashes fell out: this implies that it calls ris the hairs, which tend to fall out from much weeping, as in the story of Rabban Gamliel in Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 104b) on “she weeps sorely.” And sometimes it calls ris the skin surrounding the eye, as in the previous chapter (38a), “a ris that was pierced or split,” explained there as the outer rim of the eye.

messages.text: Gemara

When it is stated that a ḥarum is considered a blemished priest (Leviticus 21:18), this is referring to a priest whose nose is sunk. If his nose retreats, i.e., it is very short and contracted upward, or if his nose is blocked, or if his nose is so long that it droops, from where is it derived that he is considered blemished? The same verse states: “Or a ḥarum.” The term “or” serves to include all blemishes of the nose.

verse.he: כִּי כׇל־אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ מוּם לֹא יִקְרָב אִישׁ עִוֵּר אוֹ פִסֵּחַ אוֹ חָרֻם אוֹ שָׂרוּעַ׃
verse.en: No one at all who has a defect shall be qualified: no man who is blind, or lame, or has a limb too short or too long;

notes.he: למעלה בין עיניו:
notes.en: Gemara. Sunk: above, between his eyes.

notes.he: רטיי"ה שקצר באורכו:
notes.en: Soled [retreats]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) short in length.

notes.he: נסתמו נקביו:
notes.en: Bolem [blocked]: its nostrils are stopped up.

notes.he: ארוך ותלוי מלמטה משפתו:
notes.en: Notef [drooping]: long, and hanging down below his lip.

notes.he: בין עיניו:
notes.en: His nose is sunken: between his eyes.

notes.he: שנכוץ ראש חוטמו למעלה:
notes.en: Soled: the tip of his nose is drawn up.

notes.he: שסתומין נקבי חוטמיו:
notes.en: Bolem: his nostrils are stopped up.

messages.text: A ḥarum is only one who can paint both of his eyes as one.
@Rabbi Yosei You have gone too far in limiting your definition of a ḥarum.
messages.quote: A ḥarum is only one who can paint both of his eyes as one

notes.he: יותר מדאי אמרת אע"פ שאינו משוקע כל כך הוי חרום:
notes.en: You have gone too far: you have said too much; even if it is not sunken so much, he is a ḥarum.

notes.he: כלומר חלקתה על דברי חכמים כלומר דרבנן סברי אע"ג שאינו שוקע כ"כ שיכול לכחול ב' עיניו כאחת אלא פחות שוקע הוי מום. וקיימן כסידרייהו דחזי משתיהן במקום אחד:
notes.en: They said to him: you have gone too far: that is, you have departed from the words of the Sages; for the Rabbis hold that even if it is not so sunken that he can paint both of his eyes as one, but sunken less, it is a blemish. And [the eyes may] stand in their proper order, yet he sees with both of them in one place. [This last line seems to look ahead to the mishna’s case of one who sees the room and the upper story as one, discussed on 44a.]

messages.text: The Sages’ answer to Rabbi Yosei continues on 44a.
